reference.source: ICHD-3 / International Classification of Sleep Disorders
clinicalPearls: Characterised by recurrent episodes of profound hypersomnia lasting days to several weeks, during which the patient may sleep the majority of each day
Episodes feature cognitive disturbance with a dreamlike sense of derealisation, apathy, confusion and slowed thinking
Behavioural changes such as hyperphagia and, in some patients, disinhibited hypersexuality occur during episodes
Between episodes sleep, cognition, mood and behaviour return to normal
It most often begins in adolescence with a male predominance, and episodes are frequently triggered by infection or alcohol
The disorder is typically self-limiting, with episodes becoming less frequent and eventually resolving over years
Diagnosis rests on the recurrent stereotyped pattern after excluding other medical, neurological and psychiatric causes
reference.pathophysiology: The cause of Kleine-Levin syndrome is not established, but the episodic nature and the frequent infective trigger suggest a transient, possibly immune-mediated or inflammatory disturbance affecting hypothalamic and thalamic circuits that regulate sleep, appetite and behaviour. Functional imaging during episodes has shown reduced activity in thalamic and other regions, supporting a reversible functional disturbance rather than a fixed structural lesion.
additionalDifferentials: Depression with hypersomnic features or bipolar depression
Encephalitis or another structural hypothalamic lesion
additionalInvestigations: Detailed episode history and a sleep diary documenting the recurrent pattern
Polysomnography and multiple sleep latency testing, ideally comparing periods within and between episodes
MRI brain to exclude a hypothalamic or thalamic structural lesion
Screening for infection, metabolic disturbance and substance use around episode onset
Psychiatric assessment to exclude a primary mood disorder
redFlags: Focal neurological signs or persistent deficits between episodes
A first episode in later adulthood or an atypical, non-remitting course
Fever, meningism or other features of central nervous system infection
Evidence of a structural hypothalamic lesion on imaging
reference.prognosis: The natural history is generally favourable, with episodes tending to shorten and become less frequent over several years before remitting, although the unpredictability of relapses causes considerable disruption to education and work.
pitfalls: Dismissing episodes as psychiatric illness or malingering in an adolescent
Missing an encephalitic or structural cause at first presentation
Failing to counsel about the episodic, self-limiting nature and about safety during episodes
Over-investigating between episodes when examination is normal
references: International Classification of Sleep Disorders, 3rd edition (ICSD-3)
Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine (Kryger, Roth, Dement)
management: Supportive care during episodes in a safe, low-stimulation environment with supervision and reassurance
Education of patient and family about the episodic, self-limiting nature and avoidance of recognised triggers such as alcohol, sleep deprivation and infection
A trial of stimulants such as modafinil or amfetamines for disabling hypersomnolence during episodes, accepting limited benefit
Lithium considered for prophylaxis in patients with frequent or severely disruptive episodes
Practical support to protect education and employment given the disruption of recurrent episodes
Sleep medicine referral and longitudinal follow-up, tracking episode frequency as the disorder tends to remit over years
